Mortmain
MORT-mayn
n. (the holding of land by a corporation, especially a religious house, in perpetuity — literally the dead hand, because such land never falls back to the lord by death or marriage)
Anglo-French morte main, dead hand, from Latin mortua manus — land gripped by a hand that never dies and never lets go.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Mortmain is the medieval name for land held by a body that does not die. A corporation has no heir, no minority, no marriage and no death, so the feudal incidents by which a lord recovered value from his tenants never fell due, and land granted to a monastery was effectively out of the system for ever. The Statute of Mortmain of 1279 forbade such grants without royal licence, and the phrase has passed into the law of charity, where it still describes the grip of a long-dead donor's instructions on a living institution. The image is exact and Scripture has its own version. The law of Israel refused permanent alienation outright, resetting every holding in the fiftieth year: “ye shall hallow the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof: it shall be a jubile unto you; and ye shall return every man unto his possession” (Lev 25:10). The jubilee is precisely an anti-mortmain statute, and its ground is that the land is God's.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines mortmain as possession of lands or tenements in dead hands, or hands that cannot alienate; and alienate as to transfer title, property or right to another.

expand to see more

MORTMAIN, n. In law, possession of lands or tenements in dead hands, or hands that cannot alienate. Alienation in mortmain is an alienation of lands or tenements to any corporation, sole or aggregate, ecclesiastical or temporal.

ALIENATE, v.t. To transfer title, property or right to another; as, to alienate lands or sovereignty.

CORPORATION, n. A body politic or corporate, formed and authorized by law to act as a single person.

PERPETUITY, n. Endless duration; continued uninterrupted existence. The quality or condition of an estate by which it becomes inalienable.

JUBILEE, n. Among the Jews, every fiftieth year, being the year following the revolution of seven weeks of years, at which time all the slaves were liberated, and all lands which had been alienated during the whole period, reverted to their former owners.

Key Scripture

Lev 25:10 — "And ye shall hallow the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof: it shall be a jubile unto you; and ye shall return every man unto his possession, and ye shall return every man unto his family."

Lev 25:23 — "The land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me."

Luk 9:60 — "Jesus said unto him, Let the dead bury their dead: but go thou and preach the kingdom of God."

Ecc 2:18 — "Yea, I hated all my labour which I had taken under the sun: because I should leave it unto the man that shall be after me."

Modern Corruption

The dead hand: land held for ever by a body that never dies, and the jubilee that was designed to prevent it.

expand to see more

The corruption is the permanent grip of the past on the present, which is a danger to churches and charities and not only to feudal lords. An endowment made in 1280 for masses nobody now believes in still determines what a building may be used for; a trust deed written in one century governs a congregation in another. Our Lord's sharpest word about obligations owed to the dead is addressed to a man with a genuinely pressing claim: “Let the dead bury their dead: but go thou and preach the kingdom of God” (Luk 9:60).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the jubilee's reason, which is not economic policy but ownership: “The land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me” (Lev 25:23). No hand holds anything for ever because no hand owns it. The Preacher adds the builder's own frustration, that a man must leave his work “unto the man that shall be after me” (Ecc 2:18) and cannot know what he will do with it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Anglo-French morte main, dead hand; Hebrew yobel (H3104), a jubilee; Hebrew deror (H1865), liberty; Hebrew achuzzah (H272), a possession; Hebrew ger (H1616), a sojourner.

expand to see more

Anglo-French morte main — the dead hand, Latin mortua manus.

Hebrew yobel (H3104) — a ram's horn, the jubilee year; “it shall be a jubile unto you” (Lev 25:10).

Hebrew deror (H1865) — liberty, release; “proclaim liberty throughout all the land” (Lev 25:10).

Hebrew achuzzah (H272) — a possession, a holding; “return every man unto his possession” (Lev 25:10).

Hebrew ger (H1616) — a sojourner, a resident alien; “ye are strangers and sojourners with me” (Lev 25:23).

Usage

"“and ye shall return every man unto his family” (Lev 25:10) — the statute against the dead hand."

"“for the land is mine” (Lev 25:23) — why no grip is permanent."

"“but go thou and preach the kingdom of God” (Luk 9:60) — the living claim outranks the dead."
